title: The council of doom
sentences: THE COUNCIL OF DOOM
Far be it from me to pretend that I have anticipated the momentous events which are now happening; the sole purpose of the present treatise is simply
to throw light upon certain happenings of which, as far back as 1898, I was an observer and, to a modest extent, an active participant.
I have no idea what importance my notes may have for a pragmatic history of the World War; for my part, I could never reconcile myself with my conscience,
were I to keep silent, whether from caution or modesty, about facts which came into my possession by accident; yet whose historical significance may be greater,
than that I could neglect their publication with the self-serving excuse that I was not fully aware of such significance.
I am therefore making public all that I know about the matter, without reflection or criticism, perhaps loosely and unsystematically, but candidly, with names and dates.
As for the rest — how far my data may explain today's events, and how far they may cast light upon them —
I leave the judgment of this to those who understand such matters better: politicians and historians.
I shall try to be brief and stick to bare facts.
I made Rogyák's acquaintance as early as September 1898; however, this connection did not become closer until November,
when I, owing to certain administrative circumstances which need not concern us here, was placed in the sixth row of desks, fourth from the right.
Behind me, but rather to the left, sat Tivadar Zsemlye, and in front of Rogyák, Singer.
This, as we shall see, is of crucial importance to the whole affair.
The essential point, however, is that by November I was on such intimate terms with Rogyák that he would already then speak to me quite confidentially about his political views,
without my having any suspicion at that time of this interesting man's programme.
Decisive events had to intervene before it became clear to me
that what we had here was not simply a matter of convictions or opinions, but an open programme and a radical plan.
I learned of this decisive event at the end of November.
One morning I found Rogyák in excited and heated conversation with Singer.
He was leaning over the desk, whispering with lively gestures.
Singer looked very grave; he spoke little, but I felt he was making statements of vital importance.
At my arrival they suddenly fell silent.
This distrust did not offend me, for I was not yet sufficiently initiated into the matter (they remained cautious with me for some time),
to have taken a meaningful part in the conversation.
During the ten-minute break I ran into Rogyák on the corridor.
On this occasion I tactfully put a few questions to him.
He was visibly embarrassed and gave an evasive answer.
Singer was somewhat more communicative.
I learned that the Rogyák–Zsemlye affair, which had long been threatening to erupt into crisis,
had taken a turn this morning that could no longer be settled by purely diplomatic means.
I had known for some time that irreconcilable differences of principle existed between Rogyák and Tivadar Zsemlye.
Rogyák, as party chief of the radical programme, accused Zsemlye of pan-jassz aspirations — it should be noted
that at that time the jassz players had established a veritable reign of terror in Józsefváros, and their far-reaching influence was already making itself felt in Rigó Street.
Some whispered that their spies had wormed their way among us, enrolling in the fifth and sixth forms as if they were genuine Students.
Tivadar Zsemlye openly denied having any political connection with the jassz players;
such jassz acquaintances as he might have were purely of a private nature and did not harm the vital interests of Rigó Street.
Rogyák, on the other hand, several times during recess, with allusions all too easy to understand, warned
Zsemlye of the dangers of such secret intrigues; relations between them were becoming increasingly delicate.
This morning, then, quite unexpectedly, over a seemingly indifferent question, a sharp exchange broke out between the two of them in class.
On this occasion Tivadar Zsemlye, forgetting discretion in his anger, threatened Rogyák and his party followers
that at six o'clock, on the way home, jassz players armed with clubs would attack the Form.
Later, realising the extraordinary importance of his rash statement, he tried to take it back, and claimed
that he had no part in the matter, authentically knew nothing about the whole affair, and had only been told like anyone else.
Rogyák would no longer acknowledge this; he broke off negotiations with Tivadar Zsemlye at once and withdrew with Singer to hold a consultation.
Such was the state of affairs at eleven o'clock in the morning.
I reconstructed the picture of the situation from fragmentary remarks — Singer and Rogyák, feeling the responsibility of the difficult hours, spoke of the situation only with the utmost reserve.
Before eleven, during class, I received a Marconi-nudge sent across the desk from Zsemlye, in which he called upon me, under penalty of honest Injun,
to wait for him at the gate after class; he had communications of extraordinary importance for me.
Although I did not yet understand the situation well enough to see the European consequences of a possible clash
which would have broken off diplomatic relations between the jassz players and Rigó Street; instinctively I felt
that on this question I must stand with Rogyák and his friends; and to Tivadar Zsemlye's invitation to negotiate with him, I gave an evasive answer.
Rogyák, who had witnessed my loyal conduct, said nothing, but I felt that his confidence in me had greatly increased.
With that courteous but brief gravity which I have never since observed in any statesman, he later informed me that, if I had no objection,
he would welcome me at twelve o'clock in Maria Theresa Square, where he and Singer would discuss what was to be done in an "advance council-of-doom skirmish" (that is how he put it).
With a pounding heart I appeared at the appointed time and place.
The great affairs into whose focal point I had thus been thrust filled me with trembling and proud excitement — yet I tried to conceal this excitement,
seeing the grave, almost scornful composure with which these two grand personages discussed tasks of enormous scope.
Although I did not fully grasp the connections, I tried to imitate their superior, decisive manner,
secretly ashamed, but not admitting it, that I did not always understand the technical terms.
Singer began with an outline of the general situation.
Tivadar Zsemlye's statement this morning permitted the conclusion that the jassz players had committed treason (the word "treason" cropped up very frequently at this council of doom),
and thus Rigó Street at this moment found itself in a state of combat emergency, partly with Tivadar Zsemlye,
partly with those jassz players who at the beginning of the school year had secretly threatened to attack Form B with underground pistols.
This could no longer be tolerated, unless they wanted jassz players armed with knives to fall upon us one evening in the dark and take our scalps.
Zsemlye was responsible for the critical situation — at this point immediate action was required.
At Singer's words, Rogyák declared, with a carelessness that truly made one shudder,
that he was willing to fight a fatal duel with Tivadar Zsemlye, before invited tribal chiefs — but of course only in English.
He stood firm on this, and also insisted that Zsemlye should first be searched by two war lieutenants to see whether he was concealing armour — which, of course, would be treason.
Singer nodded and casually remarked that he had long been preparing for treason; and considering that his father possessed enormous underground ironworks in the Bakony,
he had already arranged for eight thousand pieces of waterproof armour to be made, which could be worn under one's singlet without anyone noticing.
The workmen had been labouring diligently for months, and within a few days the first consignment would arrive — some three thousand pieces.
Should the jassz players, through some act of treason, have learnt something of the matter and obtained armour somewhere themselves,
he had had several iron suits made for such an eventuality: iron boots, iron trousers, and a complete iron singlet.
As for the fatal duel, he also approved, with the reservation that rangers should be invited instead of war lieutenants — they were more trustworthy.
At that time I was somewhat timid, and so for a long while I did not dare to speak.
I felt, however, that my authority was sinking very low; and so, embarrassed and blushing, I too spoke up,
and raised the question whether it would not be better simply to have Tivadar Zsemlye beheaded.
For if we declared that treason had indeed taken place, there should be nothing to prevent it.
Although they showed nothing, I myself felt, surprised, that my proposal had taken the council of doom aback.
Singer replied at length, explaining that the idea in itself was not bad; the trouble was
that without a declaration of war such a thing could not be done, for this (he searched long for the expression), for this would be an ambush.
Rogyák immediately assented to this view.

He began to explain passionately that, from the standpoint of honour and character, it was impossible to set an ambush without a declaration of war (those were his words); there was a proper way to do it.
Besides, an ambush was a very delicate matter; it required a separate agreement and many conditions, all of which would have to be clarified,
and at this moment he was not entirely sure whether an ambush was permissible against jassz players; this would have to be discussed more fully with his friend
the Commander, whom he was in the habit of meeting in the evenings, and who was his adviser on difficult questions of war.
Lest treason should once again spoil everything in the meantime, however, he proposed that instead of an ambush we should launch a battle — and that immediately.
Singer assented to this.
Now only formal questions remained: above all, of course, the flag.
Singer promised to bring the flag the next day, together with the requisite rubber-stamp, which his father had had made long ago
and had kept on his writing-desk until it should be needed.
At this point another difficulty occurred to Rogyák.
"Where are we to get the mascot prey?"
he asked.
"Why, without a prey we cannot even begin the battle," as he put it.
Singer was perplexed for a moment.
Then I spoke up again and suggested that perhaps the prey might be obtained by taking up a collection.
I immediately regretted my rash interruption, for both of them suddenly fell silent, looked at each other, and smiled scornfully.
I blushed again and stammered in embarrassment that I had not meant it that way, whereupon Rogyák, in an explanatory, paternal tone,
with lofty benevolence enlightened me that the prey could not be collected, for it was a bloodthirsty animal,
and in battle it was customarily led on a chain by two constables at the head of the army, directly beside the flag.
We agreed on this.
After the consultation Rogyák administered the Oath of War to us, pledging us to commit no act of treason.
The next day at nine o'clock I interpellated Rogyák as to how we stood with regard to the war.
He replied that Singer had not received the armour, because the ship bringing the goods from the Bakony had run aground.
Later he informed me that the whole affair had to be postponed indefinitely, because before Christmas,
while we did not yet know where we stood with the documents, the whole project was not a fact on the ground.
He assured me, however, that preparations were proceeding in every direction.
The movement was spreading; the flag was indeed ready, and all America already knew of the affair.
Our alliance with California was already assured and was only waiting for the suitable moment
to launch, quite quietly and modestly, without anyone noticing, the world war.
That is all I know of the Council of Doom of 1898.
For a long time I did not concern myself with the matter.
In 1899 I enrolled in the first form of the secondary modern school, and for years other studies occupied me.
These great events have reminded me of all that I wrote.
The tracing of connections, I repeat, I leave to those better qualified than I am.
